```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 110)
library(ggplot2)
library(RColorBrewer)
pal <- brewer.pal(8, "Paired")
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 13))
```

*Session 7 of the [course](index.html) · [Slides for this session (PDF)](slides/07-hypothesis-testing.pdf)*

**Learning goals.** After this lesson you can

- state null and alternative hypotheses and draw the rejection region of a test;
- compute a test statistic and a p-value by hand and check them with R;
- explain, using a simulation, what the significance level $\alpha$ controls.

## The logic: how surprising is our sample?

A hypothesis test asks: *if the null hypothesis were true, how surprising would
a result like ours be?* We decide in advance what counts as "too surprising".
That is the significance level $\alpha$, and it defines the **rejection region**
of the test statistic.

For a two-sided z-test at $\alpha = 0.05$, the rejection region is the outer 5%
of the standard normal distribution:

```{r rejection-region}
alpha <- 0.05
z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)
curve_data <- data.frame(x = seq(-4, 4, 0.01))
curve_data$y <- dnorm(curve_data$x)

p <- ggplot(curve_data, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(curve_data, x < -z_crit), fill = pal[5]) +
  geom_area(data = subset(curve_data, x >  z_crit), fill = pal[5]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = pal[2]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = round(c(-3, -z_crit, 0, z_crit, 3), 2)) +
  labs(x = "z", y = "Density")
p
```

## A two-sided z-test, step by step

Suppose a population is normal with known standard deviation $\sigma = 1$, and
we test

$$H_0: \mu = 0 \qquad H_1: \mu \neq 0.$$

We draw a sample of $n = 50$ (in this simulation the true mean is in fact 0.2):

```{r z-sample}
set.seed(132)
x <- rnorm(50, mean = 0.2, sd = 1)
```

By the central limit theorem, $(\bar{x} - \mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})$ follows a
standard normal distribution if $H_0$ is true:

```{r z-stat}
z <- (mean(x) - 0) / (1 / sqrt(50))
z
z_crit
```

```{r z-plot}
p + geom_segment(x = z, xend = z, y = 0, yend = dnorm(z),
                 colour = "darkred", linewidth = 1.2)
```

The test statistic lies in the rejection region, so we reject $H_0$. The same
decision follows from the p-value, the probability under $H_0$ of a result at
least as extreme as ours:

```{r p-value}
p_value <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
p_value
```

Because the test is two-sided, extreme results in either direction count, and
the tail probability is doubled. Using `abs(z)` makes the formula work whether
$z$ is positive or negative.

## One-sided t-tests

When $\sigma$ is unknown we use the t distribution.

**A left-sided test.** A chocolate factory claims that its bars weigh at least
40 grams on average. An inspector weighs a random sample of 20 bars:
$\bar{x} = 38.5$, $s = 3.1$.

$$H_0: \mu \ge 40 \qquad H_1: \mu < 40$$

```{r left-test}
t_stat <- (38.5 - 40) / (3.1 / sqrt(20))
t_crit <- qt(0.05, df = 19)
c(t = t_stat, critical = t_crit, p = pt(t_stat, df = 19))
```

```{r left-plot}
t_data <- data.frame(x = seq(-3.5, 3.5, 0.01))
t_data$y <- dt(t_data$x, df = 19)
ggplot(t_data, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(t_data, x < t_crit), fill = pal[5]) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_segment(x = t_stat, xend = t_stat, y = 0, yend = dt(t_stat, 19),
               colour = "darkred", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "t", y = "Density")
```

The rejection region is in the left tail, because only small sample means count
as evidence against $H_0$. The statistic falls inside it: we reject $H_0$.

**A right-sided test.** Now $H_0: \mu \le 40$ versus $H_1: \mu > 40$, with
$\bar{x} = 41$, $s = 4$, $n = 20$:

```{r right-test}
t_stat <- (41 - 40) / (4 / sqrt(20))
c(t = t_stat, critical = qt(0.95, df = 19), p = 1 - pt(t_stat, df = 19))
```

The statistic does not reach the critical value, so we do not reject $H_0$.
Not rejecting is not the same as showing that $H_0$ is true: the sample is
simply not informative enough to rule it out.

## Two kinds of error

A statistical decision is always made under uncertainty, so errors are
unavoidable. Suppose we test whether the average birth weight of newborns in a
hospital exceeds a reference value $\mu_0$ ($H_0: \mu \le \mu_0$ versus
$H_1: \mu > \mu_0$). Whatever we decide, we can be wrong in one of two ways:

| | $H_0$ is true | $H_0$ is false |
|---|---|---|
| **Reject $H_0$** | Type I error (false positive), probability $\alpha$ | Correct decision (true positive) |
| **Do not reject $H_0$** | Correct decision (true negative) | Type II error (false negative), probability $\beta$ |

The significance level fixes the risk of a Type I error in advance. The risk of
a Type II error depends on the true effect and the sample size; $1 - \beta$ is
the **power** of the test.

## What does the significance level control? A simulation

If $H_0$ is true and we test at $\alpha = 0.05$, how often do we wrongly reject
it? We simulate 10,000 studies in which the null hypothesis is true:

```{r type-1}
set.seed(1)
p_values <- replicate(10000, t.test(rnorm(30, mean = 0, sd = 1), mu = 0)$p.value)
mean(p_values < 0.05)
hist(p_values, breaks = 20, col = pal[1], border = "white",
     main = "p-values when the null hypothesis is true", xlab = "p-value")
```

About 5% of the studies reject $H_0$ even though it is true. These are **Type I
errors**, and $\alpha$ is their long-run rate. The histogram also shows
something students rarely expect: when $H_0$ is true, p-values are spread
evenly between 0 and 1.

## Try it yourself

1. Change the true mean in the last simulation from 0 to 0.3. What proportion
   of studies now reject $H_0$? This proportion is the **power** of the test.
2. Repeat exercise 1 with samples of 10, 30 and 100. How does power depend on
   the sample size?
3. Imagine running 20 independent tests on data where every null hypothesis is
   true. Using the simulation result, how many "significant" results would you
   expect? What does this imply for studies that test many outcomes?
